content.text: Students share their reflections on how the unit has shaped their thinking.
Sharing stories builds community and deepens empathy.
Unit 1 Lesson 45 Student Edition
Performance Task handout
Express and respond to ideas about reading, writing, and sharing stories.

Reflect on how listening to classmates’ stories changed your understanding by using reflective frames and cause/effect connectors. You will also respond to peers’ ideas with clear evidence from Author’s Chair and/or
Look Both Ways
Students will express and respond to ideas about reading, writing, and sharing stories.

Students will reflect on how listening to classmates’ stories changed their understanding by using reflective frames and cause/effect connectors. Students will respond to peers’ ideas with clear evidence from Author’s Chair and/or
Look Both Ways
Turn and Talk
Reflect and Respond Dialogue
Turn and Talk
Directions:
You are going to
turn and talk about
one memorable moment from yesterday’s presentations. Use your homework responses to guide your discussion.
What was a moment that stood out to you from yesterday’s presentations? What was one moment that helped you feel empathy for a character?
My classmate _______ read a section about _______. It was memorable for me because _______.
One moment that helped me feel empathy for a character was _______.
Reflect-and-Respond Dialogue
Directions:
Today, we will use
Reflect-and-Respond Dialogue

to reflect on the Author’s Chair presentations. This community dialogue uses the Ask/Build/Challenge/Clarify routine. This means we will respond to one another’s stories using sentence frames that help us practice empathy and active listening. This speaking and listening work will strengthen your ability to share your own voices and honor others during your final presentation.
In the
Reflect-and-Respond Dialogue
, we can use sentence frames to track and articulate our ideas:
One memorable part of the presentations yesterday was when ________. It was memorable because ________.
Hearing other people share parts of their stories made me feel ________ because ________.
Sharing stories builds community/deepens empathy by ________.
One thing I learned about a classmate is ________.
One lesson I learned from this unit is ________.
You will work in different pairs, each time using the sentence frames to guide your conversations. Include the following in your second discussion and every discussion after that:
One idea from a previous conversation was ________. This made me think ________.
Let’s practice a round of dialogue.
Partner A: One memorable part of the presentations yesterday was when someone shared about being scared to ride the bus. It was memorable because I remember being scared the first time as well.

Partner B: That moment was memorable for me too. I appreciated the strong vivid description of the bus that helped me put myself in the narrator’s shoes. Hearing people share other parts of their stories made me feel connected because I understood their perspective, even if I didn’t always have the same experience.

Partner A: I heard you say you felt connected, even if you didn’t have the exact same experience. Sharing stories really helped me feel empathy for my classmates, because it helped me see the world through their eyes.
Partner B: Yeah! One thing I learned from this unit is that you never know what someone is going through until you hear it from them. We all have big moments.
Partner A: I agree. I learned about that when Josephine shared the story about her mom’s illness.

One idea from a previous conversation was that stories help people connect to shared experiences, like how so many of us can imagine being scared on the bus. This made me think of how all the vignettes in
Look Both Ways

reference a school bus falling from the sky. So many characters thought about this same image. It seemed silly at first, but it connected all of them in a memorable way. I wonder how many of my classmates think about the same things I think about!
Explain to a partner how reflecting on what we have learned can deepen your understanding.
Reflection
Reflect on your ability to notice and respond to specific moments in your peers’ presentations using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in using evidence from a peer’s story to explain why a moment was memorable or meaningful?
Community Dialogue Reflection
Reflect-and-Respond Dialogue
Based on the performance task rubric, what do you need to do to score a 3 in this Reflect and Respond Dialogue?
Directions:
Begin your conversations. Move to a new partner as indicated by your teacher
Checklist
As you participate today, try to:
Use the sentence frames to help you share your ideas clearly.
Paraphrase or refer to something a classmate said in their story.
Point to specific evidence from Author’s Chair or
Look Both Ways
to support your thoughts.
Build on or respond to your classmates’ ideas.
Keep eye contact and show that you are actively listening.
Reflection
Directions:
Think for a moment about the importance of sharing and listening to stories.
How does sharing stories help people understand one another?
Circulate through the classroom as students talk. Listen for specific references to student narratives. As you observe, ensure that each student speaks in response to the prompt.

reference a school bus falling from the sky. So many characters thought about this same image. It seemed silly at first, but it connected all of them in a memorable way. I wonder how many of my classmates think about the same things I think about!
Support students in using the Reflect-and-Respond Dialogue protocol to express ideas precisely, build on peers’ thinking, and reference specific evidence from presentations or the anchor text.
● Validate multiple interpretations as long as students ground ideas in a real detail and respond respectfully to peers.
● Name the routine explicitly: Ask → Build → Challenge → Clarify (students should know what move they are practicing).
● Model 1 “clean” exchange that includes: a specific moment, a feeling word, and a why-because explanation.
● Require students to add a “carry-forward” line starting in Round 2: “One idea from a previous conversation was ___; this made me think ___.”
● Post and practice 3 anchor stems that will be used repeatedly (1 for Build, 1 for Challenge, 1 for Clarify).
● Revoice vague statements into precise ones: “It was sad” → “I felt ___ because the line ___ showed ___.”
● Press for evidence: “Which exact detail from the excerpt made you think that?”
● Upgrade connectors: “and” → “because / as a result / therefore” to show thinking clearly.
● “At first I thought ____. Now I understand ____ because ____.”
● “One idea from a previous conversation was ____. As a result, I now think ____.”
● “I agree with you that ____, and I want to add ____.”
● “I hear you saying ____. Can you clarify what you mean by ____?”
● “I see it differently because ____. One detail that supports my idea is ____.”
● If students summarize with no reflection → Prompt: “Add: At first I thought… Now I understand… because…”
● If students can’t reference evidence → Prompt: “Name the presenter + the moment (or the vignette) and quote/describe 1 specific detail.”
● If students only agree → Prompt: “Add 1 gentle challenge: ‘Could it also be that…?’”
● Student uses at least 1 reflective frame accurately.
● Student uses at least 1 cause/effect connector to explain thinking.
● Student references a specific peer story or Look Both Ways moment (not a general statement).
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say
: As we discuss, think about how telling our own stories connects us to others by helping us find common ground.
Reflection
Reflect on your ability to notice and respond to specific moments in your peers’ presentations using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in using evidence from a peer’s story to explain why a moment was memorable or meaningful?
Students will review the protocol for the Reflect and Respond Dialogue.
Community Dialogue Reflection
(30 minutes)
Teach: Reflect-and-Respond Dialogue

Emphasize that this is a structured discussion where students are responsible for both speaking clearly and listening actively. Review the Performance Task handout, highlighting the rubric so students understand what success looks like. Clarify timing (about 4 minutes per round) and explain that students will rotate partners to practice multiple perspectives. Remind students that they may discuss a passage from
Look Both Ways
or from a personal narrative.
Lead students in a brief discussion about the rubric.
Ask:
Based on the performance task rubric, what do you need to do to score a 3 in this Reflect and Respond Dialogue?
I need to use the sentence frames well and respond directly to my classmates’ ideas. I need to listen actively and ask follow-up questions. I should stay on task and take the assignment seriously.
Say these Directions:
Begin your conversations. Move to a new partner as indicated by your teacher
Support students in sustaining a community dialogue that builds empathy by listening actively, building on ideas, and showing how stories shape understanding.
● Encourage students to draw from their own experiences while keeping the focus on the text/presentations (share what you’re comfortable sharing).
● Set a timer for rotations (about 4 minutes each) and post the round focus:
Round 1: “One memorable moment was…”
Round 2: “At first I thought… now I understand…”
Round 3: “This connects to community/empathy because…”
● Require 1 evidence move each round: a named detail from a classmate’s excerpt or from
Look Both Ways
● Circulate and prompt “Build” and “Clarify” moves when talk stays surface level.
● Coach carry-forward language in Round 2+: “One idea from a previous conversation was…” (Students must include it.)
● “One memorable part was when ___; it mattered because ___.”
● “At first I thought ___; now I understand ___ because ___.”
● “This helped me realize ___, which changed my thinking about ___.”
● “Can you clarify what you meant by ___?”
● “Could it also be that ___?”
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“I felt empathy because ___.” / “___ said ___, which made me think ___.”
Expanding:
“Building on ___’s story, I noticed ___, which shows that stories shape understanding because ___.”
Bridging:
“Building on ___’s story, I noticed ___, which connects to belonging by ___; listening to this changed my thinking because ___.”
● Revoice to include academic vocabulary: “I felt bad” → “I felt empathy because…”
● Press for precision: “She was nervous” → “The detail ___ suggests she was nervous because ___.”
● If students struggle to start → Prompt: “Use the stem exactly, then add 1 detail.”
● If students dominate talk time → Prompt: “Switch roles: Speaker A = 30 seconds; Speaker B = 30 seconds; then questions.”
● If students forget to build on prior rounds → Prompt: “Stop and add 1 carry-forward sentence before you continue.”
● Student references a peer’s story with a specific detail.
● Student uses at least 1 build/clarify/challenge move appropriately.
● Student uses cause/effect language to explain how a story changed understanding.

As dialogue rounds conclude, highlight key speaking and listening behaviors you observed. Name specific strengths (e.g., effective use of sentence frames, paraphrasing a peer, clear cause/effect reasoning) to help students internalize expectations. If time allows, invite 1–2 students to share a strong dialogue move they noticed in a peer, referencing evidence from the conversation.

Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to support and expand student use of academic language, and provide scaffolding as needed.
Emerging:
Names a classmate's story and an emotional response using a frame.
Expanding:
Reflects on how listening shifted their thinking using reflective frames and connectors.
Bridging:
Reflects on a shift in thinking using academic reflective language; cites specific peer ideas; explains cause / effect.

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Building on others’ ideas
Provide “Talk Moves” cards or sentence frames:
“I heard you say _____.”
“Can you say more about _____?”
“That connects to when _____ shared _____.”
“I agree/disagree because _____.”
Struggling with: Referring to evidence
Prompt students to begin at least one response with:
“When you shared…”
“In your story about...”
“In
Look Both Ways,
Model one example as needed:
“When Josephine shared the story about her mom’s illness, it helped me understand _____.”
Ready for extension: Evaluating their own perspective
Prompt students to challenge their own perspectives
Ask:

Is there another way to see that moment? Could there be a different perspective on that experience? How might someone else interpret that story? I interpreted Josephine’s story as a caution that we never know what someone else is going through. Someone else might interpret it as emphasizing the importance of family when getting through hard times.
Teacher Tip

Build in a brief self-assessment moment after each dialogue round. Ask students to rate their use of discussion skills (e.g., building on ideas, using evidence, active listening) using a simple visual tracker (1–3 scale, icons, or color shading). Then prompt students to set a specific goal for the next round (e.g., “In the next conversation, I will ask one follow-up question”). For multilingual learners, highlight one language move (e.g., build, clarify, or evidence) and encourage students to track their use of that move across rounds. This supports students in monitoring both content understanding and language development over time.
Checklist
As you participate today, try to:
Use the sentence frames to help you share your ideas clearly.
Paraphrase or refer to something a classmate said in their story.
Point to specific evidence from Author’s Chair or
Look Both Ways
to support your thoughts.
Build on or respond to your classmates’ ideas.
Keep eye contact and show that you are actively listening.
Help students synthesize across multiple conversations to name patterns about empathy, belonging, and perspective change.
● Honor different viewpoints: students can disagree with a pattern if they cite a counterexample respectfully.
● Collect 2–3 “pattern statements” from the class (common emotions, common turning points, common community actions).
● Ask students to support each pattern with 1 concrete example (presenter + moment/detail).
● Prompt a final synthesis statement tied to the Essential Questions.
● “Across several stories, we noticed a pattern of ___.”
● “One example that supports this is ___, when ___.”
● “This suggests ___ about empathy/community because ___.”
● “As a result, I now think ___ about sharing stories.”
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“One story showed ___.” / “Many stories had ___.”
Expanding:
“Across several stories, we noticed that ___, which suggests ___.”
Bridging:
“Across several stories, a pattern is ___; this suggests that empathy/belonging is shaped by ___, especially when ___.”
● Turn examples into patterns: “One story…” → “Across several stories, we noticed…”
● Upgrade precision: “a lot of people” → “several presenters / many narratives”
● Press for effect language: “This shows…” → “This suggests/indicates… because…”
● If students give only a theme word → Prompt: “Add 1 example and 1 because.”
● If examples don’t connect to the pattern → Prompt: “Which word/line/action proves your pattern?”
● Student states a pattern + supports it with a specific example.
● Student uses an academic verb (suggests/indicates/reveals) accurately.
● Student connects the synthesis to empathy, community, and belonging.
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Names one example from the rotations using a frame.
Expanding:
Identifies a pattern across two or more stories using synthesis language (across, throughout, several).
Bridging:
Synthesizes patterns across multiple conversations; names common turning points or community actions and explains their significance.
Community Dialogue Reflection (SL.6.1, SL6.1.a)
Students will participate in the Reflect and Respond Dialogue.
Reflection

Begin by framing reflection around Essential Question 2: “How does sharing stories help people understand one another?” You may wish to model a response that references evidence from a peer’s story, uses a reflective frame, and explains why it matters. Remind students to connect the discussion to community and empathy and to use sentence frames to articulate their thinking.
Say these Directions:
Think for a moment about the importance of sharing and listening to stories.
Ask:
How does sharing stories help people understand one another?
Optional Sentence Starter:
Sharing stories helps people understand one another by ____.”
Sharing stories helps people understand one another by giving people a window into the world that someone else is living.
Students will reflect on Essential Question 2.

standards.description: Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.
Engage in extended written exchanges with peers and collaborate on complex written texts on a variety of topics, using technology when appropriate.
Engage in short written exchanges with peers and collaborate on simple written texts on familiar topics, using technology when appropriate.
Engage in longer written exchanges with peers and collaborate on more detailed written texts on a variety of topics, using technology when appropriate.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.

How does sharing our stories help build community and empathy?
